Who handles property tax in Maricopa County

One office values, the other bills. The Maricopa County Assessor decides what each parcel is worth, assigns its class and mails the yearly Notice of Value. The Maricopa County Treasurer mails the bill, takes your payment and divides it among the 1,800-plus taxing districts, which include the state, county, cities, towns, schools, community colleges and special districts.

  • Treasurer: Suite 100 at 301 West Jefferson Street, Phoenix, AZ 85003, with customer service at 602-506-8511.
  • Assessor: 602-506-3406.
  • Online: search parcels and pay on the Treasurer's website. Sign up for eNotices to go paperless, using the authorization code on your bill.

Fake texts, calls and letters steering people toward unusual payment methods are a known problem. Pay only through the county's website or to the address on your statement.

Property taxes on a Maricopa County home

The 2020 census counted 4,420,568 residents in the county, and 63.0% of occupied homes were owner-occupied. Two houses valued the same can still get different bills, since each school district, city, fire district and special district sets its own rate. Pull up your own parcel rather than trusting a neighbor's number.

Due dates and penalties

The county bills in two halves. A.R.S. 42-18052 puts the first due date at October 1 and the second at March 1, with late status beginning after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and May 1. Tiny bills, $100 or less, come due in one piece on October 1 and go late after December 31. When a cutoff falls on a weekend or holiday, it rolls to the next business day.

The next May 1 falls on a Saturday in 2027, and subsection D then pushes the cutoff to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day. Late tax accrues 16% a year in simple interest under A.R.S. 42-18053, and a partial month is billed as a whole one. Settle the full year by December 31 and none of it applies.

How the tax lien process works

Delinquent accounts follow a calendar the Treasurer publishes. January brings an advertising fee on unpaid taxes, and February brings an online lien auction. Delinquent notices go out in June for the first round and again in December for a second round, after the second half turns late on May 1. Buyers at the auction receive certificates of purchase, and December 31 is the final day to buy subsequent taxes and assignments.

Where does the lien come from? A.R.S. 42-17153. Each January 1 it attaches to the property for that tax year, sitting ahead of other liens except state liens and liens for taxes of other years. It lasts until the tax, interest and charges are paid, a tax-sale purchaser takes title, or a certificate of removal and abatement is issued.

Sellers should pay the first half before the new year begins. Whatever remains will be settled from your sale money in any case.

Appealing your Maricopa County valuation

Expect the Notice of Value in the mail between January 1 and March 1. When you think the full cash value or class is off, you have 60 days from the mailing date to send the Assessor a Petition for Review of Real Property Valuation. Owners and their representatives may file online. Limited property value can't be appealed; full cash value and classification can.

  • Assessor: all appeals get an answer by August 15.
  • State Board of Equalization: you have 25 days from the Assessor's decision, and a hearing officer listens to both sides.
  • Superior Court: choose tax court or small claims, and file by December 15 of the notice year or 60 days after the last administrative ruling. Small claims is open to owner-occupied residential property and anything valued under $2 million.

Tax is computed from limited property value alone. It can climb 5% a year at most, unless you add to the property, remove something or change how it is used. Bought a house after December 15, and the previous owner skipped that year's appeal? You may still go to court. The 60-day window is written in A.R.S. 42-16051.

Exemptions and relief

On its homepage the Assessor lists a personal exemption for the 100% service-connected disability exemption, and changes to disabled-veteran exemptions are slated for 2027 under the state budget. Read that page before leaning on an older rule. The office also takes rental registrations online and offers virtual appointments.

Programs for widows, widowers, disabled owners and senior valuation each have their own forms, dollar limits and deadlines. Phone the Assessor at 602-506-3406 for the current versions.

Before listing, gather what an agent or buyer will ask about: your latest Notice of Value, the most recent tax bill and proof of any exemption you hold. An owner-occupied home and a rental are classed differently, so a house you rented out in the past should be checked against the registration on file with the Assessor. Getting that sorted before an offer arrives avoids surprises at closing.

Selling with taxes owed

Recording the deed moves ownership on the Assessor's records, but the lien for the current year has been in place since January 1. When you close, the title company requests the balance from the Treasurer and pays it from your proceeds. A fall sale makes one question urgent: has the first half been paid? A half left delinquent at closing has been gaining 16% a year from the day it went late.

A workable routine: request a payoff for your expected closing date, pass it to the title company early, then compare the settlement statement with that figure. If closing slips, the payoff changes, so ask for a fresh number. A cash sale doesn't wipe out the lien, though a faster close does mean less interest on a late half.

One more item: when a foreclosure sale brings in more than the debt, the surplus can go unclaimed. The Treasurer's website lists excess proceeds that a foreclosing attorney deposited under A.R.S. 33-812.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Maricopa County property tax deadlines?

Payments split into October 1 and March 1 installments. The first installment is late once the clock passes 5:00 p.m. on November 1 (November 2 in 2026), the second after May 1. A single full-year payment over $100 on or before December 31 avoids interest.

How much interest accrues on a late Maricopa County bill?

Sixteen percent a year, simple, starting at the delinquency date, with any partial month billed whole. Statute A.R.S. 42-18053 waives it for full-year payments by December 31 and for delinquencies caused by county error.

What is the deadline to appeal a Maricopa County valuation?

Sixty days from when the Assessor mailed the Notice of Value. Use the Petition for Review of Real Property Valuation, online or paper. A further appeal to the State Board of Equalization must come within 25 days of the Assessor's ruling.

Which office answers questions about my Maricopa County tax bill?

Dial 602-506-8511 for the Treasurer about balances and payments, and 602-506-3406 for the Assessor about value, class and exemptions.

Does unpaid property tax block a Maricopa County home sale?

No. Because the lien dates from January 1, the title company simply deducts the balance from what you receive at closing. Request a payoff for your actual closing date, as a late half keeps growing.

Pima County tax offices

Tucson hosts both offices. Property is valued and classified by the Pima County Assessor, who also takes appeals and runs the valuation relief programs. The Pima County Treasurer mails statements, collects payments and sells tax liens on delinquent accounts. Because the Treasurer can't change a bill unless the Board of Supervisors directs it, a dispute over value starts with the Assessor.

  • Treasurer: 240 N. Stone Avenue, lower level of the Pima County Public Service Center, Tucson, AZ 85701. Weekday hours are 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.; phone (520) 724-8341.
  • Assessor: 240 N Stone Ave, Tucson, AZ 85701, (520) 724-8630. The Valuation Relief team is at (520) 724-7500.

Due dates and penalties

Two installments are due: October 1 and March 1. Lateness begins after 5:00 p.m. on the November 1 or May 1 that follows (A.R.S. 42-18052). You'll get one statement in mid-September and no more unless the account goes delinquent, when notices on real property are sent in August and January.

Tax year 2026 has December 31, 2026 as its full-year payment date on the Treasurer's calendar. Second-half money is due March 1, 2027, and since May 1 is a Saturday the postmark cutoff is May 3, 2027. A full-year payment by December 31 of the tax year owes no interest (A.R.S. 42-18053), which means a bill still open can be cleared before year-end.

Delinquent taxes and the lien sale

Late tax accrues simple interest at 16 percent annually, with partial months rounded up. A further $5.00 or 5 percent penalty applies to anything unpaid before January. The delinquent lien is then offered at the Treasurer's tax lien sale during the last week of February, skipping Tuesday because the Board of Supervisors meets that day.

Whoever buys the lien holds a claim against your property. After three years from the sale date, that buyer can foreclose and take it. These points affect a sale.

  • After the sale, no partial payments are accepted by the Treasurer. You owe everything, delinquent taxes, interest, penalties and fees, at once.
  • Ahead of a sale, the smallest payment covers tax, interest and fees on one delinquent installment, which is a half-year.
  • A single lien can be sold for all delinquent taxes on a parcel combined (A.R.S. 42-18104).

Ways to pay the Treasurer

Three channels are open: web, mail and the counter. The web option takes ACH or electronic check and sets a floor of $10 or 10 percent of the installment due, whichever is larger. Its convenience fee is kept wholly by the payment servicer.

  • Mail: enclose the coupon and a check, cashier's check or money order in US funds, addressed to PO Box 29011, Phoenix, AZ 85038-9011. Put your state code or reference number on the check. Cash must never go in the mail.
  • Counter: cash, check or card. Cards, credit or debit, add a 2 percent service fee.
  • Wire: phone (520) 724-8341 beforehand.

A lender that escrows your taxes can ask the Treasurer for statement information, as can a tax service company. The liability is for the calendar year, January through December, though the second installment comes due the next year.

How a bill is calculated

The formula takes limited value, times the assessment ratio, times the combined rate, over $100. Do it once for primary and once for secondary, then add. Primary covers day-to-day operating costs and applies to the limited cash value, whereas secondary funds special districts like fire districts plus voter-approved bonds and budget overrides.

The rate on your bill blends every jurisdiction covering your address, for example the City of Tucson, Pima County and your school district. Two line items deserve a closer look.

  • Primary Tax Reduction: a credit against the school district's primary levy on owner-occupied homes, often called the homeowner's rebate. The state repays the district for eligible amounts.
  • Fire District Assistance: a countywide tax on every taxable property that supplements fire districts, levied under A.R.S. 48-807.

Levies and rates are outside the Assessor's control. Take a rate complaint to the political subdivisions named on your bill.

Appealing your valuation

Your petition to the Assessor is due 60 days from the Notice of Value's mail date (A.R.S. 42-16051). Those notices are mailed by March 1. A Notice of Change mailed by September 30 opens a separate supplemental appeal. An assessment appeal tries to show that the property was valued improperly, given the wrong class, or assigned an incorrect limited value. It isn't a complaint about higher taxes.

The petition must state a valuation method with supporting data.

  • Market approach: show what a comparable property nearby sold for, or what yours did.
  • Replacement cost approach: include the cost to build or rebuild plus the land value.
  • Income approach: include the information A.R.S. 42-16052 requires.

Factual errors go through a Notice of Claim, and a Notice of Proposed Correction may reach you by certified mail in any month. Keep paying the tax as billed while an appeal is pending. A lower tax brings back the overpayment plus interest at the Arizona Department of Revenue's rate; a higher one gives you 60 days to pay the increase interest-free.

Exemptions and relief

Qualifying owners can have limited assessed value reduced or frozen through Valuation Relief, and each program sets strict statutory tests for the applicant and household. Applications are due March 1 each year; later ones need a Redemption Waiver form under A.R.S. 42-11153.

A featured program is the exemption for a veteran rated 100 percent service-connected disabled. H.B. 2792, signed February 12, 2026, clarified A.R.S. 42-11111 as an emergency measure covering tax year 2026 onward. Applicants need an honorable discharge, a VA benefit summary letter showing the 100 percent rating, and income under the limit. It covers one primary residence. Current forms are available at (520) 724-7500 or ASRValRelief@pima.gov.

Selling with taxes owed

Pima County is home to an estimated 1,074,685 people, and 65.2 percent of housing units are owner-occupied. Selling while tax is open? Get a payoff from the title company with interest counted to closing, and ask the Treasurer if a lien has already been sold on your parcel. A sold lien changes the payoff, because partial payments stop being accepted.

A routine that works: find out which installments are open on your parcel, request a payoff dated to closing, pass it to title, and compare it with the settlement statement. A cash buyer's speed limits how much interest accrues, though every delinquent amount, penalties and fees included, is still taken from your proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Pima County property tax due dates?

October 1 and March 1 are the due dates, with delinquency after 5:00 p.m. on the following November 1 and May 1. In 2026 the full year is due by December 31, 2026, and second-half payments need a May 3, 2027 postmark.

How much interest accrues on late Pima County taxes?

Sixteen percent a year, simple, beginning at the delinquency date, with any partial month billed whole. Tax unpaid into January adds $5.00 or 5 percent. Paying the full year by December 31 avoids interest.

How does the Pima County tax lien sale work?

In the last week of February the Treasurer sells liens on delinquent taxes. The owner keeps the house until the lien buyer forecloses, which is allowed three years after the sale date.

Is online payment available for Pima County property tax?

Yes, through ACH or electronic check, at the greater of $10 or 10 percent of the installment as a minimum. Mail to PO Box 29011, Phoenix, AZ 85038-9011, or pay in person at 240 N. Stone Avenue, Tucson.

Who handles questions about a Pima County valuation?

The Assessor, at (520) 724-8630. Only the Board of Supervisors can direct the Treasurer to change a bill. Petition within 60 days of the Notice of Value mail date and keep paying the bill as issued meanwhile.

Who sends the bill

Two Pinal County offices share the work. The Assessor decides what your property is worth and how it is classified. The Treasurer bills, collects and then passes the money along to the school districts, fire districts, cities and towns, and community college that tax your parcel. You get one bill covering all of them.

Bring value, legal class, mailing address and exemption questions to the Assessor. Bring balance, payment and late-payment questions to the Treasurer. The Treasurer isn't required to mail a statement under Arizona law, so a bill that never arrives is no excuse for a missed due date.

Due dates and penalties

Pinal County splits any bill above $100 into two payments. Half one comes due on October 1, and it turns late once 5 p.m. on November 1 goes by. Half two comes due on March 1 and turns late after 5 p.m. on May 1. Should a late date land on a weekend or holiday, you get until 5 p.m. the next business day. The clock runs on Florence office hours, so a satellite office may close earlier.

Small bills of $100 or less are paid all at once on October 1 and stay clean until the end of December 31. Larger bills can also be settled in one payment by December 31, which spares you interest on the first half (ARS 42-18053). Once a half is late, simple interest of 16 percent a year applies, and even a few days into a month are charged as the whole month. The Treasurer expresses that as 1.33 percent per month.

A narrow break exists for owners who just paid off a loan. If the board of supervisors approves, the Treasurer may forgive interest and penalties on a delinquency that happens within twelve months of a mortgage or deed of trust being satisfied or released. Each property qualifies once. Call the Treasurer to see if yours does.

Pinal County market context

Pinal County is one of Arizona's fastest-growing counties. Headcount reached 539,380 by July 1, 2025, a 26.6 percent leap from 425,993 in April 2020. Of all housing, 81.7 percent is lived in by its owner, and a typical owner-occupied home was worth $349,000 over 2020 to 2024. Those are county-wide medians. A parcel in Apache Junction, Casa Grande, Maricopa or an unincorporated stretch near Florence can sit far from them, so judge your own Notice of Value, not the average.

How to appeal your valuation

Your Petition for Review has to reach the Pinal County Assessor within 60 days of the day your Notice of Valuation went out in the mail. Name the full cash value you believe is right and back it with an income, market or cost approach. For the market route, cite a comparable property or a sale of your own. Your postmark is treated as the filing date under ARS 42-16051. The Assessor must mail notices by March 1 each year.

Use Form 82130R for a home and Form 82130 for commercial property, vacant land and agricultural land. There's no fee, and you can ask for a meeting. The Assessor works from sales in the previous two years, so comparables from that window carry the most weight.

  • The Assessor must rule on petitions by August 15.
  • A denial, whether full or partial, opens a 25 day window to take the dispute to the County Board of Equalization. Pinal routes these to its Board of Supervisors, because the State Board of Equalization takes them only from Maricopa and Pima counties.
  • The county board must decide by October 15, with no exceptions.
  • Tax court is the alternative, available for 60 days after the final administrative ruling. Pay the taxes before they turn delinquent, or the court throws the case out.

Look at two numbers on the notice before you file: full cash value and limited property value. Only the first can be appealed, yet the bill is built on the second, and in most cases that one can't rise past 5 percent a year. When the limited value is already under what you think the house is worth, winning the appeal won't shrink this year's tax. More detail is on the county's appeal page and appeal process page.

Exemptions and what a sale does to them

Surviving spouses who are widows or widowers, and owners with a total and permanent disability, may request an exemption from the Assessor under ARS 42-11111. Filing opens on the first Monday of January and shuts on the final day of February. New applicants appear in person; renewals may be mailed once notarized. Applications are taken at the Florence, Apache Junction, Casa Grande, Maricopa and San Tan Valley offices. Questions go to 520-866-6361.

Income and net assessed value caps apply, and they are reset every year. The current numbers come from the Assessor. The widow and widower exemption runs on a three-year cycle. The disability exemption must be filed every year.

The exemption does not follow you out of a house you sell. Passing title to a new owner is one of the events that disqualifies the property, which is then taxed from that date. A replacement primary residence gets a 60 day window to file an exemption transfer form with the assessor in whichever county holds it. If you receive an exemption and plan to sell, phone the Assessor ahead of closing.

What happens to unpaid taxes

Each February the county auctions liens that cover delinquent taxes. A bidder pays your tax and takes a lien on the parcel. The lien is what gets sold, and the house stays yours. The Treasurer also oversees deeding a parcel to the State of Arizona after five years of delinquent taxes.

Interest keeps running while a balance sits. A sold lien must be paid off no later than closing. Request a payoff number from the Treasurer that rolls in earlier years and runs interest to your closing day.

Selling with taxes owed or due

Ask the Treasurer for your complete balance before listing the house, and pass that number to title or escrow. Look up the parcel on the Treasurer's website, then call to ask whether prior-year amounts, interest or a sold lien sit on top of the current bill. A seller who plans a cash sale can use the same figure, since a cash buyer's closing still pays off taxes from the proceeds.

  • Find out whether the fall installment, the spring installment or both are still owed.
  • Update the mailing address at the Assessor's office so the next bill reaches the buyer.
  • If you hold a widow, widower or disability exemption, tell the Assessor the home is sold.

Assessor offices are at 31 N Pinal Street, Building E in Florence; 575 N Idaho Road in Apache Junction; 820 E Cottonwood Lane in Casa Grande; 19955 N Wilson Avenue in Maricopa; and 31505 N Schnepf Road in San Tan Valley. Branch hours run shorter than the main office, so call before you drive.

Frequently asked questions

When are Pinal County property taxes due?

Half one is due October 1 and half two March 1. Each turns late after 5 p.m. on the following November 1 or May 1. A bill of $100 or less is paid once, on October 1, and is late after December 31.

What interest does Pinal County charge on late property tax?

Simple interest at 16 percent a year starts on the delinquency date, and a partial month is billed as a whole one. That is 1.33 percent a month. After a mortgage or deed of trust is released, the Treasurer may waive it once per property within a year, if the board agrees.

How long do I have to appeal my Pinal County property value?

Sixty days, counted from the day the Assessor mailed your Notice of Valuation. A postmark is enough proof of filing. The Assessor mails notices by March 1.

Can I appeal the limited property value in Pinal County?

No. Only full cash value or legal classification can be challenged. The limited value is what your tax is built on, and it generally can't grow faster than 5 percent a year.

Does a widow or widower exemption carry over when the house is sold?

No. Once title passes to another owner the exemption on that property ends. For the home you move into next, file an exemption transfer form with that county's assessor within 60 days.

Two county offices share the work. Values and classes come from the Mohave County Assessor. Bills and payments come from the Mohave County Treasurer. You'll find both inside the administration building, 700 West Beale Street, Kingman.

  • Assessor: (928) 753-0703, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday to Friday. Field offices operate in Bullhead City (1130 Hancock Street) and Lake Havasu City (2001 College Drive, Suite 93), both closed noon to 1 p.m.
  • Treasurer: (928) 753-0737, same weekday hours. Write to PO Box 712, Kingman, AZ 86402.
  • Recorder: (928) 753-0701. It records the deed that changes the owner on the tax roll.

Tax rates aren't the Assessor's call. Each taxing body, from the county and cities to school and fire districts, sets its own, and the bill itemizes them. The county holds 258,932 parcels, so give your parcel number every time you call or write.

Due dates and penalties

Expect your bill by early October; the first half is due October 1. In 2026 that half turned delinquent after November 2, because November 1 was a Sunday and weekend or holiday cutoffs move to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day. Second-half 2026 tax is due March 1, 2027, and since May 1, 2027 is a Saturday the same rule makes the cutoff Monday, May 3. A postmark counts as payment on mailed checks.

Second halfMarch 1 of the next yearAfter 5:00 p.m. on May 1

One payment covering both halves, made by December 31, wipes out the interest that began after November 1.

Late payment penalty and lien sales

Interest is 16% a year, charged by the month beginning the first day of the month (A.R.S. 42-18053). Not receiving a bill is no defense, since the county isn't required to send one.

Delinquent accounts can end up in the annual tax lien sale. Each certificate carries a $10 processing fee the buyer can't get back (A.R.S. 42-18116). The house itself isn't sold. The lien buyer simply gains the right to pursue foreclosure in Mohave County Superior Court after meeting statutory conditions.

Parcels whose county-held liens are more than five years old may be deeded to the State and sold at an online tax deed auction in March, where the winner pays the bid plus 8.5% and a $40 processing fee. A parcel somewhere in that process? The Treasurer, at (928) 753-0737, can say what is owed and where things stand.

How to appeal your valuation

File a Petition for Review with the Assessor no later than 60 days after the postmark on your Notice of Value. Notices are mailed by March 1, and the deadline is tied to that notice rather than to the tax bill.

The state's residential form, 82130R, walks through the steps. First the Assessor must decide by August 15. Disagree? Take it to the County Board of Equalization within 25 days of the mailed decision, and the Board decides by October 15. Beyond that sits Arizona Tax Court, with a filing date of December 15 of the valuation year, or 60 days after the Board's mailed decision when that falls later.

  • Explain how you reached your number. A sales approach cites what at least one similar nearby property sold for, or what your own parcel sold for.
  • Full Cash Value and classification are appealable. Limited Property Value, the figure taxes are based on, follows a statutory formula.
  • An agent can file for you only with the Agency Authorization form attached.

Board hearings are held in the Board of Supervisors auditorium in Kingman. Download the petition from the Assessor's forms page.

How a bill is figured

The formula runs Limited Property Value, times the assessment ratio, times the rate for your tax area. Limited value can't climb more than 5% a year unless the property is altered (a new pool or garage, say), and it never exceeds Full Cash Value.

Class changes the ratio. In the county's 2024 table, a primary residence was at 10%, rental or leased residential at 10% in class 4.2, vacant land at 15% and commercial property at 16.5%, and ratios change often. A house you rent out falls in class 4, and Arizona law makes you register a residential rental with the Assessor, family tenants included.

Proposition 101 caps levy growth at 2% a year, new construction aside, for cities, the county and Mohave Community College. School and fire districts aren't covered, so what you owe in district tax depends on the parcel's location.

Exemptions and relief

The Assessor handles every exemption and valuation program, and the Treasurer sends exemption questions there.

  • Widow, widower and disability exemption: for Arizona residents under property value and income limits updated each year. Disability needs certification from a medical provider.
  • Veteran disability exemption: created by a 2022 Arizona ballot measure and scaled to the VA disability rating. The Assessor's website carries a notice on a 2027 update.
  • Senior valuation protection: freezes a primary residence's limited value for three years. One owner must be 65, with at least two years in the home, and applications run January 2 through September 1. The freeze ends if you sell.
  • Tax deferral: for qualifying owners 70 or older, filed with the Assessor between January 1 and March 31. Deferred tax plus interest comes due when the property transfers.
  • State Aid to Education: a cut in the school portion of tax on owner-occupied homes.

Selling with taxes owed

First request a payoff on the parcel from the Treasurer, interest included. Hand it to the title company early, so the balance gets cleared at closing.

Online payment isn't offered for prior years. Call (928) 753-0737 for 2025 and earlier taxes; 2026 tax can be paid online, by phone or in person. Checks go to the Mohave County Treasurer with the stub or parcel number. Drop boxes in Kingman, Bullhead City and Lake Havasu City take checks and money orders, never cash.

A bill that shows up after closing can go on to the buyer, or back to PO Box 712 along with the sale date and buyer's name. Mention any deferral or valuation freeze to the title company, as both stop at sale. A cash buyer's quick close can shorten the stretch in which interest builds, though every unpaid dollar still comes out of your proceeds.

Outside the cities, permits and zoning go through Mohave County Development Services at (928) 757-0903. Recording steps are in the Mohave County recorder guide.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Mohave County property tax due dates?

October 1 for the first half, late after 5:00 p.m. on November 1. March 1 for the second half, late after 5:00 p.m. on May 1. A bill of $100 or less is payable in full on October 1 and goes late after December 31.

What interest applies to late Mohave County tax?

Sixteen percent a year, charged by the month from the first of the month (A.R.S. 42-18053), whether or not you received a bill.

How many days do I have to appeal a Mohave County valuation?

Sixty, counted from the Notice of Value's postmark, and notices are mailed by March 1. Petition the Assessor first. The County Board of Equalization comes next, within 25 days of the Assessor's decision.

Can I pay back taxes online in Mohave County?

Not for prior years. Online payment covers current-year tax only. For 2025 and earlier, call (928) 753-0737 or mail a check to PO Box 712, Kingman, AZ 86402.

Who do I call about a Mohave County exemption?

The Assessor's office, (928) 753-0703. It handles widow, widower, disability and veteran exemptions, senior valuation protection and rental registration.

Navajo County tax offices

Payments go to the Navajo County Treasurer. Values, exemptions and mailing-address changes belong to the Navajo County Assessor. Find the Treasurer's main office at 100 East Code Talkers Drive in Holbrook, in the county governmental center just south of town where State Routes 77 and 377 meet.

  • Assessor: 928-524-4086.
  • Mail: Navajo County Treasurer, PO Box 668, Holbrook, AZ 86025-0668.

All office hours are in Arizona time, and Arizona doesn't observe daylight saving time, which matters if you call from another state.

Tax calendar

Each year the county sends a single original bill, typically in mid to late September. October 1 opens payment of the first half. The next installment is payable March 1, 2027 and becomes delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on May 1, 2027. Mailing a payment with a postmark on or before the deadline avoids a penalty.

That May 1 falls on a Saturday, so call the Treasurer about weekend deadlines instead of relying on the last day.

Delinquent taxes and the lien sale

Late tax is charged 16% a year in simple interest, posted monthly on the first. By the Treasurer's arithmetic that equals 1.333% of the tax, no matter whether you pay early or late in the month. If a balance remains when January arrives, an extra $5 or 5% penalty is added.

An online auction each February sells the lien on unpaid tax. The Treasurer stresses that the property itself isn't being sold. Foreclosure becomes available to the lien buyer only three years after the sale date.

Once a lien is sold, a partial payment won't redeem it. Redemption takes everything owed, taxes, interest, penalties and fees, in certified funds such as cash, a cashier's check or a money order. The exact payoff comes from 928-524-4172.

Challenging your valuation

Your first option is a petition to the Assessor, due 60 days after the date printed on the Notice of Valuation. The other is filing straight with tax court. The notice lists your appeal deadline, and the postmark date is treated as the filing date.

  • Give your own full cash value and your method. For a market approach, cite what a comparable nearby property sold for, or what yours did. For a cost approach, give construction cost plus land value.
  • Limited Value comes from a statute, so it can't be appealed.
  • Assessor replies are mailed by August 15.
  • To go further, postmark a Board of Equalization appeal within 25 days after the Assessor's mailing date.
  • Without an administrative appeal, Arizona Tax Court filing is open through December 15 of the year the notice was sent. With one, it is 60 days from the last decision, but never beyond December 15.

A manufactured home never affixed to the land counts as personal property and gets a shorter clock, only 20 days after the valuation notice is mailed. The Treasurer can't change a tax amount unless the Board of Supervisors directs it, so start with the Assessor if a bill looks wrong.

Before listing, it helps to pull your latest Notice of Valuation and last tax bill. A buyer's agent will ask for them, and any deadline still open on your valuation is better known before you accept an offer.

How the tax is figured and who sets rates

To compute primary tax, multiply limited value by the assessment ratio and the primary rate, then divide by $100. Run the same steps with the secondary rate for secondary tax; the sum is your total. Operations are paid by primary tax, while special districts and voter-approved bonds and budget overrides are paid by secondary tax.

County supervisors set the county rate, plus the library district, public health service district, flood control district and fire district assistance rates. Every city, town, school district and special district chooses its own, and Northland Pioneer College sets the community college rate. A.R.S. 48-807 makes Fire District Assistance a countywide levy that hits all taxable property.

State Aid to Education trims the school district's primary tax by up to $600 on owner-occupied primary residences and mobile homes.

Selling a house and paying the tax

At closing, the title company divides the year's tax on the settlement statement, crediting the buyer with your share. The Treasurer won't divide it between owners, since the tax attaches to the property and not a person. Read the statement and ask about anything that looks off.

If your mortgage company pays the tax, it can request tax information from the Treasurer. Payment history is also posted under the Taxes tab of the Property Information page. Once you've closed, send any bill to the new owner or mark it sold and return it.

Card and e-check payments for the current year run through the county's payment website or Point and Pay, 877-459-6499. They carry a transaction fee that the county doesn't keep, and 5 to 7 business days may pass before online records show them. For earlier years, phone 928-524-4172, because the Treasurer may need to confirm amounts the website hasn't caught up on.

For a seller the sequence is simple. Look up the parcel, request a payoff dated to closing, forward it to the title company, and match it against the settlement statement. Keep your payment receipts, and confirm that nothing remains unpaid under your name. A cash buyer may want proof of payment sooner than a lender would, so having the Property Information page history ready speeds things up.

Navajo County property context

Navajo County counted 106,717 residents in 2020 and 56,180 housing units, of which 34.4% were vacant. Owners lived in 70.9% of the occupied homes. Tax notices aren't forwarded, so give the Assessor your new mailing address, at 928-524-4086, the moment it changes. Deed steps are in the Navajo County recorder guide.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Navajo County property tax due dates?

The whole year can be paid by December 31, or in two halves. October 1 starts the first half, which is delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1. March 1 starts the second, delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on May 1.

How much interest does Navajo County charge on unpaid tax?

Sixteen percent a year, simple, which the Treasurer states as 1.333% a month. An extra $5 or 5% penalty applies to tax still open when the new year starts. A missing bill doesn't waive interest.

When is the Navajo County tax lien sale?

Normally online, on the second Wednesday in February. The sale covers the lien, not the property, and a buyer may start foreclosure only after three years.

What is the appeal deadline for a Navajo County valuation?

Petition the Assessor within 60 days of the notice date on your Notice of Valuation, or file directly with tax court. For a Board of Equalization appeal, postmark it within 25 days of the Assessor's mailing date.

Will the Navajo County Treasurer divide the tax between buyer and seller?

No. Your title company does that at closing, giving the buyer credit for your share. The tax follows the property, so review the settlement statement.

Who handles property tax in Yavapai County

Property tax here is split between two county offices. Value comes from the Assessor, who appraises every parcel. Billing and collecting belong to the Treasurer, who then passes the money to the county, Yavapai College, schools, fire districts, special districts and city governments. The Board of Supervisors sets tax rates after the taxing districts submit their budgets and levies each August.

The Treasurer's Office has a counter in Prescott at 1015 Fair Street, 2nd floor, phone (928) 771-3233, open every weekday morning and afternoon, from 8:00 a.m. until 5:00 p.m. The Cottonwood Annex, 10 S 6th Street, phone (928) 639-8123, keeps shorter hours: Monday through Thursday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., with a closure from noon to 1:00 p.m. and none at all on Friday. Email goes to web.treasurer@yavapaiaz.gov. For valuation and exemption questions, call the Assessor at (928) 771-3220.

Your bill carries a four-digit tax area code. Every parcel in the same code pays the same mix of jurisdictions, which always includes the county, the community college and one or more school districts, and may add a city, fire district or improvement district. Two houses a few miles apart can therefore carry different rates, and a house in Chino Valley, Camp Verde or Sedona can sit in a different tax area from one in Prescott Valley. Find the code printed on your own bill.

Due dates and penalties

The year's tax is split into two payments. A.R.S. 42-18052 puts one due October 1 and the other the next March 1, and a payment is late once 5:00 p.m. passes on November 1 or May 1 respectively. A weekend or holiday pushes the start of lateness to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day.

DateWhat happens
By March 1Assessor mails Notices of Value
End of SeptemberPaper tax notices mailed
December 31, 2026Last day to pay the full year with no charged interest
February 9, 2027Next online tax lien auction
May 3, 2027, 5:00 p.m.Second half delinquent (May 1 falls on a Saturday)

The Treasurer cannot change or extend statutory due dates, and the payment system will not take money before bills are calculated in late September.

After delinquency, tax accrues simple interest at 16 percent annually, and a partial month is billed as a whole one (A.R.S. 42-18053). Interest is avoided in two situations: full-year payment by December 31 of the tax year, or a delinquency the assessor or treasurer caused. The treasurer, with Board of Supervisors approval, may also waive interest a single time per property if the delinquency came within a year of a mortgage or deed of trust being released.

How to pay a Yavapai County tax bill

Four ways to pay exist: online, phone, mail and counter. The online and phone channels run through Certified Payments, and the fees go to that vendor, not to the Treasurer. Phone payments use 1-866-493-0416.

  • Electronic check: $0.40 per transaction, and one e-check can cover several parcels
  • Debit card: 1 percent of the amount, minimum $1.25
  • Credit card: 2.19 percent of the amount, minimum $1.25
  • Mail: Yavapai County Treasurer, 1015 Fair St., Prescott, AZ 86305, with the parcel number on the check
  • In person: at the counter in Prescott or in Cottonwood

Payments by mail post in three to five business days; electronic ones post within three. Pay the exact amount, because an overpayment is refunded. Owners who want paper bills replaced can register at eNoticesOnline with the authorization code on the front of the last bill.

Liens and tax lien auctions

What you owe also works as a lien on the property. Per A.R.S. 42-17153 it arises on January 1 of the tax year and ranks above other liens and encumbrances, except state liens and liens for other years' taxes.

Yavapai County runs an annual online tax lien auction, and the next is set for February 9, 2027. Properties deeded to the state for back taxes are offered separately on the Board of Supervisors' Tax Deed Sales page. A seller with delinquent years should remember that interest runs at 16 percent and the lien sale happens each February.

How to appeal a valuation

Your Notice of Value, mailed by March 1, prints a filing date for a Petition for Review to the Assessor, and the window runs 60 days from the postmark. Petition forms are available from the Assessor's website during the filing period or at either Assessor office, and they come with instructions.

  • Notice of Change: mailed by September 30 for new construction, additions, splits or changes in use. The County Board of Equalization hears it, and you must file within 25 days of mailing. A state-certified hearing officer hears the appeal.
  • Tax Court: if you disagree with the Assessor or the Board, file within 60 days of the Board's decision or by December 15, whichever is later.
  • Skip the administrative step: you may file directly in Tax Court, but no later than December 15 of the valuation year.
  • Buyers: if you bought before December 15 of the valuation year, you may appeal to Tax Court by that date. Later, the new owner has until December 15 of the levy year.

Before you file, gather evidence. Recent sales of similar houses near yours, photos of defects, a repair estimate and any appraisal you paid for all carry weight. Describe the problem in one or two plain sentences on the petition, such as a wrong square footage or a classification that no longer fits how the house is used. Keep a copy of everything you send and note the date you mailed or delivered it.

Full Cash Value is the appealable figure. Your tax is actually computed from the Limited Property Value. That figure can climb only 5 percent a year unless the property changed, and 95 percent of Yavapai parcels fall in that group.

Questions to settle before you list

A few quick checks save trouble later. Find your tax area code and confirm which school and fire district it names, since buyers compare monthly costs between houses. Look at the Limited Property Value on your last Notice of Value, because it shows what the next bill is likely to resemble. Check that no exemption you hold will end when the house changes hands, since the buyer starts fresh and must file for any benefit they qualify for.

If a mortgage is being paid off at closing, the lender's payoff letter and the tax payoff are two separate figures, and both are deducted from your proceeds. Review each one on the settlement statement and ask the escrow officer to explain any line you do not recognize before you sign.

Sellers who live out of the area can handle most of this by phone and email. Ask the title company which documents can be signed before a notary near you, and confirm in advance where the closing papers will be mailed so a missed envelope never holds up funding.

Write down the parcel number, the amount of the last payment and the date it posted. With those three items, a title company can answer a buyer's lender within a day instead of a week, and your closing date stays firm.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Yavapai County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Exemptions and relief programs

Personal exemption applications are taken in person at either Assessor office on weekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Filing opens on the first Monday in January and closes on the last business day of February. Exemptions cover widows and widowers, totally and permanently disabled persons, disabled military service members and their surviving spouses.

The rules for a disabled service member are changing. Someone with a 100 percent service-connected disability, or total disability based on individual unemployability, gets a full exemption on the primary residence starting with tax year 2026, with income limits still applying that year. Legislation passed in 2026 removes the income limit beginning with tax year 2027. Others who qualify receive the annual exemption amount the state sets. The Senior Freeze program closes to applicants on September 1.

Applying early in the season is wise, because a missing document can be fixed while the filing window is still open. If you are selling in the same year, tell the buyer which benefits your house currently carries so their first bill does not come as a surprise.

Owner-occupied homes already receive a State Aid reduction on the primary school district tax, shown on the bill, and the state reimburses the school districts. Ask the Assessor at (928) 771-3220 which documents to bring, including an Arizona driver's license and a VA award letter for a disability claim.

Selling with taxes owed

Before listing, find out from the Treasurer what the parcel owes, and plan to clear it through escrow at closing. The county's tax inquiry website lets you search by parcel number and view a bill. Whoever owns the house while taxes are due is responsible for them. A bill arriving after closing goes to the buyer or the buyer's lender.

Market prices help here. The 2026 median single-family price is $539,000 through October, down from $555,000 in 2025, so check the tax area on your bill and compare your house with recent sales near it.

At a normal closing the title company asks the Treasurer for a payoff, both sides sign, escrow deducts the open amount from your proceeds, and the deed is then recorded. Bring your latest tax notice and parcel number.

If you are selling a house that has been sitting vacant or was inherited, look at the last two bills before you do anything else. Missing notices are the usual reason an owner learns of a delinquency late, and a mailing address that was never updated sends bills to the wrong place. The Treasurer can update the address on the account, and the title company will ask for proof that earlier years are current before it schedules a closing. A cash buyer will also want the balance in writing, so request the figure early and keep a copy for your file.

Frequently asked questions

When is the second half of Yavapai County property tax due?

The second installment comes due March 1. Under A.R.S. 42-18052 it is late after 5:00 p.m. on May 1, and since May 1, 2027 is a Saturday, lateness starts at 5:00 p.m. Monday, May 3, 2027. Paying the full year by December 31 means no charged interest.

How much interest does Yavapai County charge on late property tax?

Simple interest of sixteen percent annually, with a partial month treated as whole (A.R.S. 42-18053). No interest applies if you pay the entire year by December 31 of the tax year, or if the lateness traces to a mistake by the assessor or treasurer.

How long do I have to appeal my Yavapai County property value?

Count 60 days from the postmark on the Notice of Value mailed by March 1. A Notice of Change, mailed by September 30, gives you 25 days from mailing to reach the County Board of Equalization. December 15 is the usual Tax Court cutoff.

Who pays property tax when a Yavapai County house sells?

Taxes due fall on the current owner, and escrow usually pays the open amount at closing. A bill that shows up after closing is the buyer's or the lender's to pay. Start by asking the Treasurer what the parcel owes.

Can I pay Yavapai County property tax by credit card?

Yes. Certified Payments charges 2.19 percent with a $1.25 minimum for credit cards, 1 percent with a $1.25 minimum for debit cards, and $0.40 for an electronic check. The fee goes to the vendor, not the Treasurer. Pay online from the Treasurer's page or call 1-866-493-0416.

Once a bill is delinquent, interest accrues at 16 percent a year, simple, and a part-month counts as a full month (A.R.S. 42-18053). You can cut it off by paying the whole year before December 31 of the tax year. A delinquency caused by a county mistake carries no interest at all.

An owner who has just paid off a mortgage and then falls behind can ask for a one-time interest waiver, which needs approval from the county board of supervisors.

Sellers sometimes list in spring without realizing how the bill calendar shapes the closing. The lien for the year begins January 1. A closing in the middle of those dates means one half may be paid and the other not. A cash purchase adds no lender timeline on top of this, so the tax payoff is often the only item on the schedule that depends on a county office.

Fast closings work best when the figures are ready early. A buyer who pays cash and skips an appraisal can sign within days, which only helps if you already know what the Treasurer will want. How to challenge your valuation

The yearly notice of value is your starting point, and state law has the assessor mail it before March 1 (A.R.S. 42-15101). If you disagree with it, you have 60 days from the mailing date to file a petition for review, and a postmark is accepted as the filing date (A.R.S. 42-16051).

In the petition you give your own view of full cash value and explain how you got there. A comparable property works, and so does the recent sale of your house. Separately, when a data error touched a group of properties, the assessor may amend notices within 60 days of mailing. Past that point the roll changes only through an appeal.

Call the Assessor's Office to confirm the dates on your own notice, because the mailing date shifts from year to year.

Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. A quick call to (928) 679-8188 or (877) 500-1818 confirms it before you drive over.

What interest do late Coconino County taxes carry?

Sixteen percent a year, simple. It is not collected if the full year is paid by December 31 or if a county error caused the delinquency.

How long do I have to dispute the assessor's value?

Two months, in practice: the window is sixty days from the mailing date of the notice, and your postmark is your filing date.

Can I close on a Coconino County house with an unpaid tax bill?

Yes. Because the bill is a lien, escrow settles it at closing out of your proceeds after getting the balance from the Treasurer.

Assessor, Treasurer and who to call

Two county offices share the work, and they sit together at 197 S. Main Street in Yuma, AZ 85364. The Yuma County Assessor sets each parcel's value and its class. The Yuma County Treasurer, in Suite 203, mails the bills and takes the payments.

  • Assessor: 928-373-6040 or assr-info@yumacountyaz.gov, for value, land use class, exemptions and petitions.
  • Treasurer: 928-539-7781 or treasury@yumacountyaz.gov, for statements, payments, delinquent accounts and the February lien sale.
  • Board of Supervisors: 928-373-1010. It hears appeals as the board of equalization and keeps the list of state tax-deeded parcels.

Rates and levies are not the Assessor's call. School districts, cities, fire districts and the county set them, so a bill that feels too big is best raised at their budget hearings.

The local market in brief

Yuma County, in the southwest corner of Arizona, had 203,881 residents in 2020 and an estimated 224,449 in July 2025. The city of Yuma is the seat and largest city, with San Luis, Somerton and Wellton also inside the county. Typical owner-occupied homes were valued at $217,800 in the 2020 to 2024 figures, and 71.0 percent of homes are owner-occupied.

Farming is the main employer. The county leads Arizona in crop sales, and the winter vegetable season from November to March fills much of the nation's demand for leafy greens. That seasonal rhythm means plenty of sellers are working around harvest-season jobs and schedules.

Due dates and penalties

Tax is collected in two installments. October 1 is the first due date and March 1 the second. A late charge starts after 5:00 p.m. on the following November 1 or May 1, and a weekend or holiday pushes that cutoff to the next business day. For 2026 the November cutoff landed on Monday, November 2, so any 2026 first-half balance is now accruing interest. The second installment is due March 1, 2027.

DateWhat happens

  • Late interest runs 16 percent yearly, not compounded, and each started month is billed as a full month.
  • Interest is waived when the county office caused the delinquency by mistake, and when you pay the entire year before December 31 ends.
  • Taxes still delinquent on January 1 pick up a 5 percent penalty.
  • The Treasurer, with the Board of Supervisors' approval, can forgive interest and penalties one time per property if the delinquency follows within a year of a paid-off mortgage.

Not receiving a statement is no defense. Anyone who pays their own tax and has no statement by October 15 should call the office or use the portal at yumacountyaz.gov/paytaxes.

How the tax lien affects a sale

Each year's tax becomes a lien on January 1. It outranks every other lien on the parcel except state liens and liens for other years' taxes (A.R.S. 42-17153). So an unpaid bill rides into escrow with the house. Your closing agent should request the Treasurer's payoff number well before closing.

If your lender pays through an impound account, confirm with the servicer that the county actually received the money. Buyers should also give the Assessor their name and mailing address so bills reach the right person.

Classification matters to the next owner. Code 3.01 means an owner-occupied primary residence, which already receives the Less State to Education reduction from the Treasurer. Rental use is code 4.02. To change the code, the buyer files an Affidavit of Primary Residence with the Assessor and attaches proof of residence such as an Arizona driver's license, ID card, voter registration card or state income tax return. Until one of those arrives, the class stays put.

How to appeal your valuation

Start with a Petition for Review sent to the Assessor. The window is 60 days from the day your notice of value went in the mail (A.R.S. 42-16051), and your notice prints the exact date. Notices are due out by March 1 each year.

  • Step one: the Assessor reviews the petition and may inspect the property. You can then request a meeting with the Assessor or a representative.
  • Step two: still unhappy? Take it to the Board of Equalization, a role the Board of Supervisors fills here. File within 25 days after the Assessor's decision is mailed (A.R.S. 42-16056). An issue left out of the original petition cannot be added.
  • Step three: tax court or superior court. December 15 is the final day for a tax court filing. Small claims procedures are open when a residence is valued under $300,000 or the tax bill is under $5,000.

Four grounds are accepted: wrong facts on the property record such as square footage, a full cash value out of line with recent neighborhood sales, an income approach showing the value is excessive, or a miscalculated limited property value. A complaint that taxes are simply too high does not qualify.

Exemptions and the senior freeze

Arizona offers a few exemptions and a valuation freeze, all processed by the Assessor. Dollar limits change yearly, so ask for the current figures before relying on any number.

  • Widow, widower and total and permanent disability exemption: the Assessor takes filings from the first working day of January through March 1. Income must stay under the statutory limit, and eligibility is renewed each year (A.R.S. 42-11111).
  • Disabled service members: a primary residence owned by someone with a 100 percent service-connected rating is fully exempt, and lower ratings earn a partial exemption. A further exemption under House Bill 4168 starts with tax year 2027, and applications open January 4, 2027.
  • Senior Property Valuation Protection Option, the senior freeze: the filing period runs from January 1 to September 1.

A sale ends these benefits. Under A.R.S. 42-11111, conveying title to another owner disqualifies the exemption. Anyone who moves has 60 days after moving in to send an exemption transfer form to the assessor in the county of the new primary residence.

Selling with taxes owed

A parcel with prior-year tax still unpaid at the end of December can be offered in the Treasurer's lien sale the following February. For 2025 taxes that sale is February 18, 2027, and paying the balance in full by 5:00 p.m. on February 17 takes the parcel off it.

The investor who buys a lien takes over the right to collect, and the lien statutes also let the Treasurer foreclose the right to redeem (A.R.S. 42-18101). A different sale is run by the Board of Supervisors for real property the state holds under a tax deed, drawn from a list prepared on or before the first Monday in November. The Board's number is 928-373-1010.

An old balance is cheapest to clear before the year turns, since December 31 ends interest-free payment and January 1 adds the 5 percent penalty. If you sell with taxes owed, the title company pays that amount out of your proceeds at closing, using the Treasurer's payoff as its guide. A cash sale can close ahead of a lien sale date, once the payoff has been confirmed.

Before you list the house

  • Search your parcel in the Treasurer's payment portal and see whether both 2026 halves show as paid.
  • Look at the class code on your notice of value.
  • If you hold a widow, disability, service-member or senior freeze benefit, ask the Assessor how it ends at sale and how to move it.
  • Once an offer is accepted, have your closing agent order a payoff statement from the Treasurer.
  • Keep the notice of value and any petition paperwork, since the buyer may ask about the value of record.

Frequently asked questions

Is the 2026 first half of Yuma County tax already late?

Yes. After 5:00 p.m. on November 2, 2026 an unpaid first half became delinquent. Interest on a full-year payment is avoided only if it arrives by December 31, so clear any balance before year end.

Can I sell a Yuma County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The lien remains on the parcel until the balance is settled at closing. Your closing agent can request a payoff from the Treasurer, 928-539-7781, covering interest through the closing date.

What interest rate does Yuma County charge on late taxes?

Sixteen percent a year, simple, charged by the month with partial months rounded up. County mistakes and full-year payment before December 31 end the interest.

How long do I have to appeal my Yuma County valuation?

Sixty days after your notice of value is mailed, and the notice prints the date. After an Assessor denial, the next appeal, to the Board of Equalization, is due 25 days from mailing of the decision.

Does selling my home end my Arizona property tax exemption?

Yes. Conveying title to another owner is a disqualifying event under A.R.S. 42-11111. If you buy another primary residence, file an exemption transfer form with that county's assessor within 60 days of moving in.

Who bills, who values, and how to reach them

Billing and collection belong to the Gila County Treasurer, while the Gila County Assessor produces the values behind each bill. On top of county tax, the Treasurer collects for the school, fire, sanitary, water, flood control and improvement districts and the city and town governments inside the county.

  • Treasurer, Globe: 1400 E. Ash, Globe, AZ 85501, phone 928-402-8702 or 928-402-8703.
  • Treasurer, Payson: 707 S. Colcord Rd., open Tuesdays and Thursdays from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.
  • Treasurer, mail: Gila County Treasurer, P.O. Box 1093, Globe, AZ 85502.
  • Assessor, Globe: 1400 East Ash Street, 928-402-8714. Assessor, Payson: 707 S. Colcord Rd., Suite 102, 928-472-7973.

If you are asking why a rate is what it is, contact the district that set it. The Treasurer's page also takes online payments.

Due dates and delinquency

A Gila County bill comes in two halves. October 1 is the due date for the first and March 1 for the second, and they turn delinquent at the close of business on November 1 and May 1 respectively, which A.R.S. 42-18052 defines as 5:00 p.m. If one of those days falls on a weekend or holiday, the county waits until 5:00 p.m. on the next business day.

Plan ahead from today. The second half of the 2026 bill is due Monday, March 1, 2027. May 1, 2027 is a Saturday, so the late cutoff for that half moves to 5:00 p.m. on Monday, May 3, 2027. A first half still sitting unpaid is already earning interest.

What paying late costs

Delinquent tax grows at 16 percent a year, simple interest, with any fraction of a month rounded up to a month (A.R.S. 42-18053). Stated monthly, that is one and one third percent added on the first day of each month.

Interest is not charged in two cases:

  • The whole year's tax is paid on or before December 31 of the tax year.
  • An error by the county assessor or treasurer caused the delinquency.

A bill that never reached you is still owed. A.R.S. 42-18054 says liability for the tax and interest holds even when neither the owner nor the lender received the statement. Because the county mails a single original bill each year, an owner whose lender pays the taxes should check that the lender asked for the bill.

How a Gila County house is valued and taxed

Each March 1 or earlier, the Assessor sends a Notice of Value. It lists two figures: Full Cash Value, which tracks the market, and Limited Property Value, which is what the tax is actually figured on. The limited value is held to growth of 5 percent a year unless the property changes, as with an addition or a split of the parcel.

A legal class on the notice sets the assessment ratio:

  • Class 3, an owner's or qualified family member's primary residence: 10 percent.
  • Class 4.1, an owner's second or non-primary residence: 10 percent.
  • Class 4.2, a residential rental: 10 percent.
  • Class 2, vacant land and other property: 15 percent.
  • Class 1, commercial and industrial: 16 percent.

Ratios may move from year to year. Rates come last: A.R.S. 42-17151 has each county, city, school and community college governing body set its levy by the third Monday in August, with tax statements mailed in late September or early October.

How to appeal your valuation

The first step is a Petition for Review to the Assessor, due within 60 days after the Notice of Value was mailed (A.R.S. 42-16051). In it you give your own opinion of full cash value and the support for it, such as a comparable property or the price you paid for your home.

Pick the right form, because a wrong or incomplete one is rejected. Form 82130R covers residential property, Form 82130 covers vacant land and commercial property, and Form 82131 covers multiple parcels. Send the completed form by mail or email to Gila County Assessor's Office, ATTN: Appeals, 1400 E Ash Street, Globe, AZ 85501.

  • The Assessor answers before August 15 of the valuation year.
  • Unhappy with the answer? File with the County Board of Equalization within 25 days of the date the Assessor sent it. The Board is reachable only after an Assessor appeal.
  • After the Board, Arizona Tax Court takes over, with 60 days from the mailing date of the hearing officer's decision.
  • A missed 60-day window is not the end. You may still go to Tax Court before December 15 of the valuation year.

The next round of Notices of Value goes out before March 1, 2027.

Property tax relief programs

Four programs run through the Assessor: exemptions for widows and widowers, an exemption for people with a disability, a veteran exemption, and the Senior Freeze. Nothing is applied automatically. The county urges people to apply even if they are unsure they qualify.

For tax year 2026 the widow, widower and disability exemption removes up to $4,873 of assessed value, for people with a total and permanent disability as well. Two caps apply. Your Arizona property overall cannot exceed $36,454 of assessed limited value, and household income from 2025 must stay at or below $39,865 with no children under 18, or $47,826 with children. A disabled veteran rated 100 percent by the VA faces no cap on the primary residence and no value limit. Applications are taken from January 2 to March 1, and a first-time applicant goes in person to the Globe or Payson office.

The Senior Freeze locks the Limited Property Value of a primary residence for three years. You qualify if you are at least 65, have lived in the home two years, and keep a three-year average income below $47,712 for one owner or $59,640 for two or more owners. The window is January 2 through September 1. Selling or renting ends the freeze, and tax rates keep applying.

Unpaid taxes and the lien sale

Each February the Treasurer offers unpaid taxes for sale as tax liens, as A.R.S. 42-18101 directs, and can then move to foreclose the right to redeem. Gila County holds this sale online. Notice of the parcels appears in the Silver Belt and the Payson Roundup.

Whoever buys a lien pays the delinquent tax, then pays each following year's tax in June until the owner redeems or the lien is foreclosed. Parcels with five years of delinquent taxes can be deeded to the State of Arizona, a process the Treasurer's office oversees.

Selling with taxes owed

Start by asking the Treasurer what is due on your parcel through your expected closing date, interest included. Next, ask the title or escrow company how the current year's bill will be shared between you and the buyer.

  • Find the parcel in the Treasurer's online tax bill search, by owner name, account number or parcel number.
  • See whether the first half of the current bill is paid.
  • Settle any balance from your sale proceeds and hold on to the receipt.

A cash buyer skips lender underwriting, so the county balance is usually the one open item. Get it early, and the closing date holds.

What is the due date for the spring half of a Gila County bill?

March 1 is the due date, and the half is late after 5:00 p.m. on May 1. On the 2026 bill that is Monday, March 1, 2027, with the cutoff moved to Monday, May 3, 2027 since May 1 is a Saturday.

Can I pay my whole Gila County bill at once?

Yes. Paying the full year's tax on or before December 31 of the tax year avoids interest under A.R.S. 42-18053.

What if I missed the 60-day window to appeal my Gila County valuation?

You can still file in Arizona Tax Court before December 15 of the valuation year. Tax Court filings go through the Maricopa County Superior Court, so do not send those forms to the Assessor.

Who qualifies for the Senior Freeze in Gila County?

An owner who is at least 65, has lived in the primary residence for two years, and has a three-year average income under $47,712 for one owner or $59,640 for two or more owners. Applications run January 2 through September 1, and renewal is needed every three years.

Where do I pay Gila County property tax?

Online through the Treasurer's payment portal, in person at 1400 E. Ash in Globe, in Payson at 707 S. Colcord Rd. on Tuesdays and Thursdays, or by mail to P.O. Box 1093, Globe, AZ 85502. The Treasurer's direct line is 928-402-8702 or 928-402-8703.

The petition should name the full cash value you believe is right and support it. The law allows three approaches: income, market (citing at least one comparable property or the sale of your own), or cost, which adds building cost to land value.

Missed the Assessor deadline? The Arizona Tax Court still takes an appeal of full cash value before December 15 of the valuation year, and those papers should not go to the Assessor's office. If property tax goes unpaid

Tax left unpaid can end in a lien sale. A county treasurer in Arizona may auction a delinquent lien to the public, and Apache County posts the liens online before an auction held each February.

The incorporated places are the city of St. Johns and the towns of Eagar and Springerville. Other named communities are mostly census-designated places.

Gathering your records for a sale

A seller with a clear paper trail closes faster. Start with the Notice of Value, which shows how the Assessor sees the property, and the most recent tax notice, which shows what each half costs. Print the Treasurer's account page for the parcel so you have a dated record of what was paid.

Write down the date of every call and the name of the person who answered. If a figure from the Treasurer or Assessor later differs from the title company's number, those notes show where each one came from and help you settle the difference fast.

If the house sits on possessory rights land or near reservation land, call the Assessor early, since the Assessor counts improvements on possessory rights as real property. Keep any deed, lease or correspondence together so a buyer and title company see the same story.

A balance can be cleared at closing. Get the payoff from the Treasurer, hand it to the title company and have it paid out of your proceeds. If a lien has already been sold to an investor, ask the Treasurer how redemption works.

16% a year, prorated monthly. Ask the Treasurer what your parcel owes.

Sixty days from the Assessor's mailing of your notice of valuation, using a petition under A.R.S. 42-16051. After that, the Arizona Tax Court is still open before December 15 of the valuation year.

Who handles property tax in Santa Cruz County

Two offices split the work here. The Assessor assigns each parcel a value and a legal class, and the Treasurer collects. To pay in person, visit the Treasurer's office, found in Room 104 at 2150 N. Congress Drive in Nogales and open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. For mail, write to PO Box 1150, Nogales, AZ 85628, and make checks payable to the Santa Cruz County Treasurer. The Assessor also controls exemptions and the mailing address printed on your bill.

One bill stacks up the rates of every body that taxes the parcel: the county, the school district, the fire district and other special districts. Primary taxes pay operating costs. Secondary taxes pay for special districts, bonds and voter-approved overrides. To work out primary tax, multiply limited value by the assessment ratio and by the primary rate, then divide by $100. Secondary tax is figured the same way. Owner-occupied homes get a State Aid to Education credit against school primary tax, and every taxable parcel carries a countywide Fire District Assistance tax under ARS 48-807.

Due dates, interest and penalties

Any bill above $100 comes in two installments. Installment one falls due October 1, and it counts as late when postmarked or received after 5:00 p.m. on November 1. Installment two falls due March 1, with lateness starting after 5:00 p.m. on May 1. If the whole bill is $100 or less, it all comes due with installment one. Pay both installments in full before 5:00 p.m. on December 31 and the interest on the first one is waived. The county mails statements in mid-September, with one coupon per installment. You won't hear from it again unless a payment lapses.

After a deadline passes, interest starts at 16 percent a year, prorated at 1.333 percent per month, and it makes no difference whether you pay on the first or last day of that month. A $5 penalty is added to taxes still unpaid when January arrives. Partial payment of a delinquent tax lien isn't allowed. The least the county will accept is the tax, interest and fees owed on the late installment.

The county counted 50,020 residents on July 1, 2025, which is 4.9 percent more than in April 2020. How to pay your bill

Four ways to pay: online, phone, mail or the counter. The county's card vendor, Point&Pay, charges $3.95 on debit cards, 2.5 percent on credit card payments over $100 and $2.00 on smaller credit payments. An electronic check costs $2.50. The Treasurer receives none of these fees and is barred by law from charging a processing fee. An online payment takes three to four business days to post. Mailed payments must be a personal check, cashier's check or money order. Cash is never mailed.

To see the current year's balance, search the parcel on the county's property information site and open the taxes tab. For earlier years, call the Treasurer at 520-375-7580, since extra charges may not appear online. Mortgage and tax service companies can request statements from the Treasurer, and you may receive an information statement as a courtesy. If the amount shown for an installment looks off, call the Treasurer.

How to appeal your valuation

Use Form 82130, the Petition for Review of Real Property Valuation, and file it with the Assessor. Valuation notices are mailed by March 1, and the clock is 60 days from that mailing. The county's FAQ frames the period as March 1 through April 29, and blank petitions are available at the Assessor's office. Under ARS 42-16051, the petition gives your own figure for full cash value and rests it on an income, market or cost approach.

The Assessor also changes mailing addresses, so ask for yours to be updated when you sell. The Assessor's number is 520-375-8030. If your petition is denied, the next stop is the County Board of Equalization, then court, on the deadlines printed in the decision.

Exemptions for widows, widowers and disabled owners

The county lists exemptions for qualifying widows, widowers and disabled persons. Applications are yearly, accepted from January 1 through the last working day of February. The Assessor, at 520-375-8030, can walk you through them. ARS 42-11111 also covers disabled former service members.

Conveying title to another owner ends an exemption, so tell the Assessor after closing. A move to a new primary residence gives you 60 days to file a transfer form with that home's county assessor.

What happens to unpaid taxes

Unpaid tax is sold as a lien at the delinquent tax lien sale, held each February. Investors bid the interest rate down from 16 percent in 1 percent steps, and a zero percent bid is allowed. Once three years pass from the sale date, the purchaser of the lien may foreclose and acquire the property. The county describes this as selling a lien, not the home.

Clear the tax and any lien before closing. Call the Treasurer for a payoff figure, at 520-375-7980 for lien questions or 520-375-7580 for prior-year balances, and give it to the title or escrow company.

Taxes when you sell

  • Look up the current balance in the parcel search and phone the Treasurer about earlier years.
  • Find out if an installment is still open and if interest has piled up.
  • Once title passes, ask the Assessor to switch the mailing address and drop any exemption.

Nogales, Rio Rico and Patagonia houses all answer to the same county offices, though the district rates that make up each bill vary by address. Settling the balance first helps a cash sale close quickly, because no buyer's escrow has to chase down a missing payoff figure.

Installment one is due October 1 and installment two March 1. Late status begins after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and May 1 respectively. Small bills of $100 or less are paid with installment one.

Can I avoid interest on the first installment?

Yes. If both installments are paid in full ahead of 5:00 p.m. on December 31, the county drops the interest on the first one.

What is the penalty for late property tax in Santa Cruz County?

Sixteen percent annual interest accrues, prorated at 1.333 percent monthly, and taxes still open in January pick up a $5 penalty. The February lien sale is where unpaid taxes end up.

Where do I pay property tax in person in Santa Cruz County?

Go to Room 104 at 2150 N. Congress Drive in Nogales on a weekday between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. A check can also go to PO Box 1150, Nogales, AZ 85628, and online or phone payment adds the vendor's fees.

Can a disabled former service member get a property tax exemption in Santa Cruz County?

ARS 42-11111 gives an exemption to those with a qualifying disability rating. The Assessor at 520-375-8030 can say whether you qualify, and the filing season ends on the last working day of February.

December 31, 2026Final day to pay the full year without interest
March 1, 2027Second half comes due
May 4, 2027, 6:00 p.m.Second half is delinquent

An unpaid first half is already accruing interest. Clearing the entire year before December 31 ends it, which a December seller can arrange at the closing table (A.R.S. 42-18053).
