Interest and card fees

Once a bill is delinquent, the county charges 16% a year without compounding, and even a partial month is charged in full (A.R.S. 42-18053). The Treasurer applies that 16% in monthly steps from the first of the month until payment.

Interest is off the table in three cases:

  • A mistake by the assessor or treasurer produced the delinquency.
  • The whole year is paid in full by the end of December in that tax year.
  • A mortgage or deed of trust was released the previous year, in which case the treasurer may waive interest and penalties one time for the property if the supervisors agree.

For a sale, ask the Treasurer for a payoff that holds through your closing date. Parcel search and card payments are on the Treasurer's website. Paying by Visa debit adds $4.00, a credit card adds 2.55%, and the jurisdiction code you give over the phone is 1312.

How to appeal a valuation

If the notice looks wrong, you have 60 days from its mailing to petition the County Assessor. A.R.S. 42-16051 sets that limit and treats the postmark as your filing date. Owners of record get a notice each year, and only the full cash value or the property class may be challenged.

Your petition should say what you think full cash value is and back it with real evidence. State law names three approaches: income, market and cost. For the market approach, you need a comparable property or the sale of the property in question. A recent arm's-length purchase of your own house is the best evidence you can bring.

Note that limited property value is a different figure. Proposition 117 holds its growth to 5% a year, with exceptions found in A.R.S. Title 42, Chapter 13, Article 7. Bills run on limited value, so a rise in full cash value does not always lift your tax by the same amount.

Tax relief for homeowners

The Assessor administers two programs, and its staff can quote the current income and value limits. Phone 928-669-6165 before you list.

  • The exemption for widows, widowers and totally disabled persons age 17 or over. Applicants must live in Arizona, fit within income rules, and stay below an indexed assessed-value limit. A physician must certify that a disability is total and permanent.
  • Senior Property Valuation Protection, known as the senior freeze, which holds limited property value steady for three years. The owner must be 65 when applying, live in the home as a primary Arizona residence, and meet income rules.

A value can jump when a buyer takes over a home whose prior owner held a senior freeze, so a buyer should expect a first notice of value that looks higher than the seller's. Owners of short-term rentals should also look at the rental registration form on the Assessor's page and the state's online lodging marketplace registration.

Questions to settle before you list

A little groundwork keeps the sale on schedule. With the Assessor, confirm that the owner of record is the person signing the deed, and ask whether any exemption or senior freeze is attached to the parcel, because a buyer's first notice of value may look different from yours. With the Treasurer, ask what is open for the current year and for any older years, and have the payoff dated for the day you plan to close. With the Recorder, ask what the filing will cost.

Hold on to anything that proves permits were pulled for work on the house, and for a mobile home, make sure the title has the right name on it. Hand the same set of figures to your title company so everyone works from one number. Sellers who live elsewhere should start with a phone call to the offices in Parker.

If you inherited the house

Heirs often find a tax bill addressed to someone who has died. Before you list, find out who is the owner of record and make sure the Assessor has your mailing address, so you do not miss a notice of value and the 60-day window that follows it. Ask the Treasurer for the balance and for any earlier years that remain open. If the house is a mobile home, check that the Motor Vehicle Division title has moved into your name, because the roll cannot change before that. Then give all of it to the title company at the start, not the end.

Selling with tax due

The tax lien attaches on January 1 of the tax year (A.R.S. 42-17153). Only state liens and tax liens from other years outrank it. It lasts until taxes, penalties, charges and interest are paid, a buyer takes title at a tax sale, or a certificate of removal and abatement is issued. Expect the buyer's title company to want the current year and any earlier years cleared out of your proceeds.

Owing tax is routine at a sale as long as the numbers are clear. Follow this order:

  1. Request a payoff from the Treasurer dated for your closing.
  2. Check the owner of record with the Assessor.
  3. Hand both figures to the title company.
  4. Sign the deed with its sworn affidavit of property value under A.R.S. 11-1133. The recorder must refuse the deed without it unless an exemption is noted.

For recording requirements and the current fee schedule, call the Recorder at 928-669-6136. With a cash buyer there is no lender timeline, so the county payoff is often the one open item left.

Frequently asked questions

What happens if I do not pay the first half of my La Paz County tax?

It goes delinquent and 16% annual interest starts building. Settling the whole year by December 31, 2026 stops more interest, under A.R.S. 42-18053.

Where do I pay La Paz County property tax?

Send or bring payment to the County Treasurer, 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 203, Parker, Arizona 85344, or use the website or phone. Do not plan on a Friday visit, since the office keeps Monday to Thursday hours, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Cards cost extra: $4.00 on Visa debit and 2.55% on credit.

How long do I have to appeal my La Paz County notice of value?

You get sixty days, counted from the day the Assessor mailed it. The petition goes to the County Assessor, and under A.R.S. 42-16051 your postmark is the filing date.

Does La Paz County have a senior property tax freeze?

Yes. Senior Property Valuation Protection freezes limited property value for three years. The owner must be 65 at application, use the home as a primary Arizona residence, and meet income limits. Call the Assessor at 928-669-6165 for the form and current limits.

Can I sell a La Paz County house that still has tax due?

Yes. Closing pays the lien from your proceeds. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff for your closing date, because interest runs monthly on delinquent amounts, and pass it to the title company.

Where to pay

Safford is where you pay. The County Treasurer collects for all nineteen taxing authorities in the county from the General Services Building, 921 Thatcher Blvd.

  • At the counter: staff accept cash, checks, and credit or debit cards.
  • Through the mail: send payment to P.O. Box 747, Safford, AZ 85548.
  • Drop box: look for it in the east parking lot outside the General Services Building.
  • Online: Point and Pay adds a convenience fee of 2.45 percent for credit cards (minimum $2.00), $1.50 for an electronic check, or $3.95 for a debit card.

Phone 928-428-3440 for the Treasurer when you want an amount confirmed, and 928-428-2828 for the Assessor with value questions. The online tax search updates every hour on business days and displays balances along with lien redemption amounts.

Choosing how to pay

Convenience costs money here. Paying through Point and Pay is quick, but each method carries its own fee, while the counter, the mail and the drop box in the east parking lot cost nothing extra. Whichever route you pick, keep the receipt or confirmation number for your closing file. A seller who is paying off a balance just before closing should still ask the Treasurer for the exact figure first, because a payment that falls short leaves interest on the remainder.

Due dates and interest

Each September the county mails one statement with two stubs, one per half. A late date that falls on a weekend or holiday shifts to the next business day.

Next up is the second half, due March 1, 2027. May 1, 2027 falls on a Saturday, so that half is late after 5 p.m. on Monday, May 3.

Payment or chargeRule
First halfDue October 1; late after 5 p.m. on November 1
Second halfDue March 1; late after 5 p.m. on May 1
Whole yearPaid by December 31, no interest is assessed
Bills under $100Due by December 31
Interest16 percent simple per year, added monthly on the first (A.R.S. 42-18053)

You can pay in pieces, monthly or twice a month, but interest keeps building on whatever past-due amount is left.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Graham County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

If your tax bill never arrives

Tax and interest are owed whether or not the paper bill shows up. Not receiving a statement is no ground for waiving interest, and A.R.S. 42-18054 treats liability for tax, interest, fees and penalties the same way.

If no bill has reached you by October 1, call 928-428-3440 for the amount. Compare the parcel number and description on each statement with your own records before paying, so the money lands on the right property. Owners with a mortgage should confirm that the lender requested the bill. Many lenders pull tax data straight from the county and the owner then gets an informational postcard. A lender that does not make the request leaves the statement to go to the owner.

How Graham County values property

Owners of record get a Notice of Valuation from the Assessor in the mail before March 1 each year. Since Proposition 117 took effect for tax year 2015, the Limited Property Value is the only figure used to calculate the tax, and it can rise no more than 5 percent per year.

This changes how you appeal. The tax rests on the Limited Property Value, but the only number you can contest is the Full Cash Value, the market-based one. State law produces the limited figure from last year's value or a formula, so it offers nothing to argue.

Rates are the other half of the bill. Each taxing authority on your parcel, from the county to your school district, sets its own rate, and A.R.S. 42-17151 requires levies to be fixed on or before the third Monday in August. The Treasurer's page lists current rates by taxing authority and combined rates by area. Use the Treasurer's Office for balances and due dates and the Assessor's Office for values.

How to appeal a valuation

Your appeal starts with a petition to the Assessor. File it inside 60 days of the notice date shown on the front of the Notice of Valuation. That deadline comes from A.R.S. 42-16051, which also wants your estimate of full cash value and the facts behind it.

Pick the form that matches your property from the list on the county's Assessment and Appeals page:

  • DOR 82130R for residential property.
  • DOR 82130 for commercial, industrial, vacant land and agricultural property.
  • DOR 82131 for multiple parcels, and DOR 82130NC for a Notice of Change.
  • DOR 82130AA if you want an agent to act for you.
  • DOR 82300 and its supplements, for commercial appeals based on income and expense statements.

When the Assessor's answer leaves you unsatisfied, the next stop can be the Board of Equalization, the Tax Court, or both, and the original appeal may also be filed directly with the Tax Court. Your decision letter from the Assessor names the next deadline, so open it as soon as it comes.

Relief programs

Arizona gives breaks to widows and widowers, to people with a total and permanent disability, and to honorably discharged people who served and now have a disability, plus a Senior Freeze. The County Assessor runs each one. Each exemption trims taxable value by a fixed dollar amount, and every individual exemption has a household income limit.

  • Only one individual exemption can be claimed, even by someone who fits several categories.
  • The veteran exemption changed beginning with tax years that start on or after January 1, 2026, and a new veteran application goes to the Assessor between the first Monday in January and March 1.
  • The Senior Freeze fixes the valuation of a primary residence for a renewable three years when the owner meets age and income rules. Taxes are still levied at the district rate.

Dollar limits change every year. Ask the Graham County Assessor at 928-428-2828 for this year's amounts and forms.

When taxes go unpaid

Each February the Treasurer sells delinquent taxes to an investor at a lien sale. Bidders compete on the lowest interest rate they will accept, and the winner receives a registered Certificate of Purchase.

The parcel list is posted outside the Treasurer's office, advertised in the Eastern Arizona Courier, and updated weekly in February on the county website. A lien buyer must also take assignment of any older outstanding certificates on the parcel. Anyone who owes back tax can get the exact payoff figure by calling 928-428-3440.

Selling a house in Graham County

Your title company decides who covers the current year's tax. The next statement generally lands in the buyer's name about a year after the deed is recorded, and depending on the closing date, the current year's tax may not have been assessed yet.

A titled mobile home is billed as personal property. The tax record moves only after the buyer is issued a new title, and a signature on the back of the old title leaves the roll untouched. Complete the title transfer so the following bill reaches the right person.

With a balance due, get a payoff figure from the Treasurer and hand it to the title company, which pays it out of your proceeds. A cash buyer is not waiting on a lender, so a clean tax record protects that speed.

A short pre-listing checklist

Before you put the house on the market, spend a few minutes on the tax side. Look up your parcel in the Treasurer's search and note the balance and any redemption amount. Check the notice date on your latest Notice of Valuation so you know whether the appeal window is still open. If you hold an exemption or the Senior Freeze, ask the Assessor how a sale changes it. Then give your title company the Treasurer's phone number so the payoff request can go out the day you sign the contract.

Graham County in brief

Graham County's seat and biggest city is Safford, and a portion of the San Carlos Apache Indian Reservation sits within its borders. Thatcher and Pima are the other towns. About 40,157 people live here, in 14,645 housing units. A typical owner-occupied home was valued at $212,000 for 2020 through 2024, owners live in 73.1 percent of homes, and median household income was $67,325.

Frequently asked questions

What interest does Graham County charge on late property tax?

Sixteen percent per year, simple, added month by month. Clear the full year before December 31 and no interest applies. A bill you never received does not excuse it.

Can I make partial payments on my Graham County taxes?

Yes. The Treasurer accepts partial payments monthly, semi-monthly or on your own schedule. Interest keeps building on whatever past-due balance remains.

How long do I have to appeal a Graham County valuation?

Sixty days from the notice date on the front of your Notice of Valuation. The notice is mailed before March 1 each year.

Is there a fee to pay Graham County property tax online?

Yes. Point and Pay adds 2.45 percent to a credit card payment ($2.00 minimum), $1.50 to an electronic check and $3.95 to a debit card. The counter, the mail and the drop box carry no such fee.

Who do I call about a Graham County tax balance?

The Treasurer's Office at 928-428-3440 handles balances, due dates and payment options. Call the Assessor at 928-428-2828 for values, exemptions and appeal forms.
